'''''Euonymus alatus''''', known variously as '''burning bush''', '''winged euonymus''', '''winged spindle''', and '''winged spindle-tree''',<ref name=autogenerated3>{{cite journal |last1=Wenning |first1=Bruce |title=Winged Euonymus: An Exotic Invasive Plant Fact Sheet |journal=Ecological Landscape Alliance |date=13 April 2012 |url=https://www.ecolandscaping.org/04/landscape-challenges/invasive-plants/winged-euonymus-an-exotic-invasive-plant-fact-sheet/ |accessdate=15 May 2020}}</ref> is a [[species]] of [[flowering plant]] in the [[Family (taxonomy)|family]] [[Celastraceae]], [[native plant|native]] to [[Central China|central]] and northern China, Japan, and [[Korea]].

It is a popular [[ornamental plant]] in gardens and parks due to its bright pink or orange fruit and attractive autumn color: The common name "burning bush" refers to its bright red autumn color. The [[cultivar]]s 'Compactus'<ref>{{cite web |url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/Plants/89363/Euonymus-alatus-Compactus/Details |title=''Euonymus alatus'' 'Compactus' AGM |work=RHS Gardening |publisher=Royal Horticultural Society |accessdate=23 June 2020}}</ref> and 'Fire Ball'<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/171496/euonymus-alatus-fire-ball/details | title = ''Euonymus elatus'' 'Fire Ball' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 4 October 2023}}</ref> have gained the [[Royal Horticultural Society]]'s [[Award of Garden Merit]].<ref>{{cite web  | url= https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/pdfs/agm-lists/agm-ornamentals.pdf | title = AGM Plants – Ornamental | date = July 2017 | page = 37 | publisher = Royal Horticultural Society | accessdate = 20 February 2018}}</ref>

== Description ==
[[File:Winged euonymus.jpg|thumb|right]]
This [[deciduous]] [[shrub]] grows to {{cvt|6.1|m|ft}} tall, often wider than tall. As with the related ''[[Euonymus phellomanus]]'', the stems are notable for their four corky ridges or "wings". The word ''alatus'' (or ''alata'', used formerly) is [[Latin]] for "winged," in reference to the winged branches. These structures develop from a [[cork cambium]] deposited in longitudinal grooves in the twigs' first year, unlike similar wings in other plants such as ''[[Quercus macrocarpa]]''.<ref>{{cite journal |author=Bowen |first=William R. |year=1963 |title=Origin and Development of Winged Cork in Euonymus alatus |url=https://www.journals.uchicago.edu/doi/abs/10.1086/336201 |journal=Botanical Gazette |pages=256–261 |volume=124 |issue=4|doi=10.1086/336201 |url-access=subscription }}</ref> The leaves are {{cvt|2|–|7|cm|in|frac=4}} long and {{cvt|1|–|4|cm|in|frac=4}} broad, ovate-elliptic, with an acute apex. The flowers are greenish, borne over a long period in the spring. The fruit is a red [[aril]] enclosed by a four-lobed pink, yellow, or orange capsule.
[[File:2014-11-11 14 33 05 Euonymus alatus foliage during autumn along Idaho Street in Elko, Nevada.jpg|thumb|right|Detail of leaves in autumn]]
[[File:Euonymus alatus autumn leaf.jpg|thumb|right|Detail of a leaf in autumn]]

All parts of the plant are toxic by ingestion, causing severe discomfort.<ref>{{cite web | url = https://www.rhs.org.uk/plants/6969/euonymus-alatus/details | title = ''Euonymus alatus'' | publisher = RHS | access-date = 24 October 2022}}</ref>

== Distribution and habitat ==
''Euonymus alatus''′s native distribution extends from [[Northeast Asia|northeastern Asia]] to central China.<ref name=autogenerated3/><ref name=fryer>{{cite web |last1=Fryer |first1=Janet L |title=Euonymus alatus. In: Fire Effects Information System |url=https://www.fs.fed.us/database/feis/plants/shrub/euoala/all.html |website=U.S. Department of Agriculture, Forest Service, Rocky Mountain Research Station |publisher=Fire Sciences Laboratory |accessdate=12 May 2020}}</ref> Besides central and [[East China|eastern China]], ''Euonymus alatus'' also appears in Korea, in Japan, and on the island of [[Sakhalin]] in Russia.<ref name=autogenerated2>{{cite web |title=Flora of China Project |url=http://www.efloras.org/flora_page.aspx?flora_id=2 |website=Flora of China |publisher=eFloras.org/ Beijing: Science Press; St. Louis, MO: Missouri Botanical Garden Press}}</ref> In its native areas, it occurs in forests, woodlands, and scrublands from sea level to an elevation of {{cvt|8900|ft|m|abbr=on}}.<ref name=autogenerated2 />

''Euonymus alatus'' is not native to North America. It was first introduced in the United States in the 1860s<ref name=autogenerated3/> and is found in [[New England]] and from [[Illinois]] south to [[North Florida|northern Florida]] and the [[Gulf Coast of the United States|United States Gulf Coast]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kartesz |first1=John T |title=A synonymized checklist and atlas with biological attributes for the vascular flora of the United States, Canada, and Greenland |journal=Kartesz, John T.; Meacham, Christopher A. Synthesis of the North American Flora. North Carolina Botanical Garden. In Cooperation with: The Nature Conservancy; U.S. Department of Agriculture, Natural Resources Conservation Service; U.S. Department of the Interior, Fish and Wildlife Service |date=1999 |volume=1st}}</ref> It also is found in southeastern Canada.<ref name=fireball>
{{Cite web|url=https://gpnmag.com/news/spring-meadow-nursery-unveils-first-seedless-burning-bush/ |title=Spring Meadow Nursery unveils first seedless burning bush |publisher=Greenhouse Product News 13 October 2023}}</ref>

== Uses ==
Generally cultivated for its ornamental qualities, attraction to wildlife, and ability to adapt to urban and suburban environments,<ref name=autogenerated3 /> the shrub commonly is used in foundation planting, hedges, and along highways and commercial strips.<ref name=autogenerated4>{{cite web |title=Sterile Variety of Invasive 'Burning Bush' Developed |url=https://www.farmprogress.com/management/sterile-variety-invasive-burning-bush-developed |website=Farm progress |date=26 August 2011 |publisher=University of Connecticut. |accessdate=21 May 2020}}</ref> Sales across the United States are in the tens of millions of [[United States dollar|dollars]] every year.<ref name=autogenerated4 />

The corky winged stems are used in [[Traditional Chinese medicine|traditional Chinese]] and [[traditional Korean medicine]] to treat conditions such as cancer, [[hyperglycemia]], and [[Diabetes|diabetic]] complications.<ref name=autogenerated1>{{cite journal |last1=Zhai |first1=Xifeng |display-authors=etal |title=Euonymus alatus: A Review on Its Phytochemistry and Antidiabetic Activity |journal=Evidence-Based Complementary and Alternative Medicine |year=2016 |volume=2016: 9425714 |pages=1–12 |doi=10.1155/2016/9425714|pmid=27642361 |pmc=5014951 |doi-access=free }}</ref> Chemicals that have been isolated from the plant include [[flavonoid]]s, [[terpenoid]]s, [[steroid]]s, [[lignan]]s, [[cardenolides]], [[phenolic acid]]s, and [[alkaloid]]s.<ref name=autogenerated1 />

== Invasive species ==
''Euonymus alatus'' is regarded as an [[invasive species]] of woodlands in the northeastern United States and southeastern Canada, where it can outcompete native vegetation and disrupt local [[ecosystem]]s.<ref name=fireball/><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.invasive.org/eastern/midatlantic/eual.html |title=Winged Burning Bush (''Euonymus alatus'') |work=Plant Invaders of Mid-Atlantic Natural Areas |last1=Swearingen |first1=J. |first2=B. |last2=Slattery |first3=K. |last3=Reshetiloff |date=2002 |publisher=[[National Park Service]] and [[United States Fish and Wildlife Service]]}}</ref> It is currently, since the 1970s, considered an [[invasive species]] in 21 U.S. states,{{citation needed|date=December 2024}} and its importation and sale are prohibited in the U.S. states of [[Maine]],<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://www.maine.gov/dacf/mnap/features/invasive_plants/euonymus.htm |title=Burning Bush |publisher=Maine Natural Areas Program |website=Invasive Plants |language=en |access-date=20 August 2017}}</ref> [[Massachusetts]],<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.mass.gov/eea/agencies/agr/farm-products/plants/massachusetts-prohibited-plant-list.html |title=Massachusetts Prohibited Plant List |publisher=Massachusetts Department of Agricultural Resources |access-date=4 July 2013}}</ref> [[New Hampshire]],<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.agriculture.nh.gov/publications-forms/documents/prohibited-invasive-species.pdf |title=Fact Sheet: Prohibited Invasive Plant Species Rules, Agr 3800 |publisher=New Hampshire Department of Agriculture, Markets and Food |date=31 January 2017 |access-date=30 July 2018}}</ref> [[Pennsylvania]],<ref>{{Cite web |title=Controlled Plant & Noxious Weed Lists |url=https://www.pa.gov/agencies/pda/plants-land-water/plant-industry/noxious-weeds-and-controlled-plants/controlled-plant-noxious-weed-lists |access-date=29 April 2026 |website=www.pa.gov |language=en}}</ref> and [[Vermont]].<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://agriculture.vermont.gov/sites/agriculture/files/documents/PHARM/Plant_Pest/NoxiousWeedsQuarantine1.pdf |title=Noxious Weeds |publisher=Vermont Agency of Agriculture |website=Quarantine #3: Noxious Weeds |language=en |access-date=8 October 2022}}</ref>

Dr. Thomas Ranney of [[North Carolina State University]] at the Mountain Horticultural Crops Research Station in [[Mills River, North Carolina|Mills River]], North Carolina, developed a new seedless cultivar named Fire Ball Seedless (''Euonymus alatus'' NCEA1) which became available to wholesale growers in the spring of 2024 as the first seedless cultivar of the shrub on the market.<ref name=fireball/><ref>
{{Cite web|url=https://ena.ipps.org/uploads/docs/57_139.pdf |title=Breeding Non-Invasive Nursery Crops}} International Plant Propagator's Society Combined Proceedings Volume 57</ref> Seedless cultivars could allow the phasing out of sales of seeded versions of the shrub and reduce its tendency to spread invasively.<ref name=fireball/>
